title: Can we find the primes of a multiplication without doing it?
description: Each number in three multiplications is split into its own primes, and the primes of the two numbers are joined into one row. The product is never worked out.
teaching_notes: One idea: the primes of a multiplication are the primes of its two numbers put together. Watch for students who multiply first and then struggle to factorise a big number.

video_script.why: The child writes the primes of a big multiplication by splitting each number and joining the primes, the way the book joins the primes of twelve and six to get seventy two.
video_script.substitution: the book's own multiplications: fifty six times twenty five, one hundred and eight times seventy five, and one thousand times eighty one
video_script.anchor: three multiplications, each with its two numbers split into rows of primes
video_script.payoff_line: Joining the primes of the two numbers gives the primes of the multiplication

final_answer.spoken: the rows of primes, joined, for each multiplication

maths_rules: check: the counts of each prime in the joined row are the counts in the two pieces added together
video_script.design: Each multiplication has its two numbers split in two rows of primes, one below the other. The two rows slide together into one row.

beats.on_screen: a small title card From your book; three multiplications 56 × 25, 108 × 75 and 1000 × 81 stand in a column with a question mark

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a question from your book about three big multiplications.
<bookmark mark='three'/>They are fifty six times twenty five. Then one hundred and eight times seventy five, and one thousand times eighty one.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>Can we find the prime factorisation of each without multiplying first?

beats.on_screen: the three multiplications stay on the board; Keeko sits at the corner of the board as the child

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

beats.on_screen: the row of 12 = 2 × 2 × 3 and the row of 6 = 2 × 3 slide together into one row of 72

marks.way: the rows of 12 and 6 appear side by side
marks.join: the two rows slide together into one row of primes

narration: <bookmark mark='way'/>We use the same way as the example in your book. Twelve and six each have a row of primes.
<bookmark mark='join'/>When we join the two rows, we get the primes of seventy two.

marks.given: the three multiplications are written under the word Given

narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, three multiplications, each with two numbers.

beats.on_screen: To find: the primes of each multiplication, without multiplying first
narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find the primes of each multiplication without multiplying first.

beats.colours: 2s in teal, 7 in gold, 5s in amber
narration: <bookmark mark='fifty'/>Step one, take the first multiplication and split each number on its own. Fifty six is two times two times two times seven.
<bookmark mark='twenty'/>Twenty five is five times five.

beats.colours: 2s in teal, 3s in amber, 5s in gold
narration: <bookmark mark='hundred'/>Step two, take the second multiplication. One hundred and eight is two times two times three times three times three.
<bookmark mark='seventy'/>Seventy five is three times five times five.

beats.colours: 2s in teal, 5s in gold, 3s in amber
narration: <bookmark mark='thousand'/>Step three, take the third multiplication. One thousand is two times two times two times five times five times five.
<bookmark mark='eighty'/>Eighty one is three times three times three times three.

beats.on_screen: Step 4: join the two rows of each multiplication into one row and check that the counts of each prime are added

marks.slide: the two rows of each multiplication slide together into one row
marks.count: the count of each prime in the joined row is the count in the two pieces added, and each piece is ticked as all primes

narration: <bookmark mark='slide'/>Step four, join the two rows of each multiplication into one row.
<bookmark mark='count'/>Each prime is counted as often as it occurs in the two pieces together. Every piece has only primes.

marks.ans: the three joined rows are boxed in green

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>Joining the primes of the two numbers gives the primes of the multiplication. We never had to multiply the big numbers.
